unit.title: Weld using flux cored arc welding process to FCAW

summary: This Level 3 unit teaches you to weld structural and plate work with flux cored arc welding (FCAW) to a written welding procedure specification (WPS) under the AWS code the Centre uses. You will learn to read wire classifications, choose between gas-shielded, self-shielded and metal-cored wires, set and check the parameters, do the calculations, weld groove and fillet joints in all positions, find the causes of defects, test welds and welders, control distortion, and plan, lead and record a production job safely.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). It covers **flux cored arc welding (FCAW)** to a specification: the production welding of steel frames, columns, beams, base plates, tanks and heavy brackets, in the shop and on site, where the work is inspected against a code.

FCAW uses a tubular wire filled with flux (or metal powder), fed continuously through a gun. It lays down weld metal much faster than stick welding, works in all positions with the right wire, and some wires make their own shielding so they can be used in the wind. At this level you must weld to the WPS, understand why each variable is controlled, and lead others doing the same.
**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 3 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust centres and other providers, and welders who lead FCAW work on structural steel, plate fabrication and site erection.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means on the job
rows: Work to the specification and WPS
Read the WPS, keep inside its ranges, check welders' qualifications, and stop work when a condition cannot be met.
Read wire classifications; choose gas-shielded, self-shielded or metal-cored wire; match the gas and polarity; store wire properly and trace its batch.
Set up and check the equipment
Set up the power source, wire feeder, drive rolls, liner, gun and gas; check wire speed and arc voltage with meters.
Work out wire feed speed, heat input, duty cycle, weld metal, wire needed and arc time.
Make multi-pass groove and fillet welds in the flat, horizontal, vertical-up and overhead positions (1G–4G, 1F–4F).
Apply preheat and interpass limits, and plan sequences that keep the work in line.
Recognise porosity, slag inclusions, lack of fusion, cracking and undercut, know their causes and cure them.
Inspect visually, and prepare and read bend, fillet break and macro tests.
Work safely and lead the team
Control fume, arc light, spatter, gas and electrical hazards; plan the job, brief the team, keep the weld records.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on specifications and WPSs, wire classification, self-shielded and metal-cored wire, shielding gas, equipment, parameters and calculations, out-of-position welding, joint preparation and backing, heat control, consumable control, qualification, testing, defects, health and safety, distortion, records, planning and leading the team.

A **written paper**: short answers that need exact terms or figures (for example CTWD, 4G, nozzle, backing strip, metal-cored wire, bend test, pre-flow, ceramic, duty cycle, contact tip, slag, 3F, or a worked travel speed) and essays in full sentences, with calculations set out.

**Practical tasks** done as a group: single-V butt test plates in the vertical (3G) position on a backing strip, with bend tests; and fillet welds in the vertical-up (3F) and overhead (4F) positions, with fillet break and macro checks.

blocks.note: At this level learn every setting by its effect: what happens to the arc, the bead, the fusion and the weld metal when it goes up or down. Most questions ask why something went wrong, or which choice is best for the job.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Working to the specification and the WPS

blocks.p: On coded work the client's specification names the code, and the code sets the rules for procedures, welders, inspection and acceptance. In this unit you work to the AWS code the Centre uses; refer to "the code" and to the WPS, not to memory.

head: Document
What it is
rows: The written instructions for each type of joint: base metal and thickness range, joint design (bevel, root opening, backing), wire classification and diameter, gas and flow, polarity, wire speed or current, voltage, travel speed, stick-out, positions and direction, preheat and interpass temperature, number of passes and cleaning

The record of the test weld that proved the WPS, with the actual values used and the test results. Some codes allow certain FCAW procedures to be **prequalified** (used without a PQR) if every detail stays inside the code's limits
Proof that a welder passed a test, and the process, positions and thicknesses it covers
Show which welder made each weld, with which wire batch and gas, and the inspection results

blocks.p: Some changes alter the weld metal or the fusion so much that the WPS no longer applies. These are **essential variables**: for example, a different wire classification, a change of shielding gas (or dropping the gas), a change in polarity, a different joint design, a move outside the thickness range, a new position or direction, a big change in heat input, or a lower preheat. If one must change, the work stops until a WPS that covers the change is found, or a new one is qualified and approved.

blocks.note: Never change the WPS to match what a welder "likes", and never let a welder work outside the ranges because the welds "look nicer". Stop them, reset to the WPS, and have the welds already made checked.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Each welder must hold a qualification for the process, the positions and the thickness range of the work. Generally (check the code's table):

head: Test
Generally qualifies groove welds in
Generally qualifies fillet welds in
rows: None (fillet tests do not cover grooves)

ul: A test on 10 mm plate covers a limited thickness range; a test on thicker plate (for example 25 mm) covers thicker work.
Vertical tests are done in one direction (usually up). A welder qualified vertical-up is not automatically qualified vertical-down.
A qualification lapses if the welder has not used the process for a set period (often six months).

head: AWS
ISO
Description
rows: Flat: groove or fillet welded from above
Horizontal groove: plates upright, weld axis level
Horizontal fillet: weld in the corner, axis level

sections.title: Health and safety for production FCAW

head: Hazard
Why it matters with FCAW
Controls
rows: FCAW makes much more fume than GMAW or GTAW, and self-shielded wire makes the most. The fume contains manganese and other metals that damage the lungs and nervous system over time
Extraction at the arc (hoods or fume-extraction guns); head out of the plume; respirators where extraction is not enough; ventilate enclosed areas
Too much suction pulls the shielding gas away and causes porosity
Set the suction as the maker says and check the welds
High currents give a very bright arc and strong ultraviolet
Helmet with the right shade (often about 11–13 for FCAW; follow the chart); skin covered; screens for others
Vertical and overhead work drops hot slag and spatter onto the welder
Flame-resistant jacket or sleeves, cap, closed collar, done-up cuffs, leather gloves; trouser legs over boots
High open-circuit voltage; wet sites; sweat
Dry gloves; sound cables and guns; work lead clamped close to the joint; machines with a voltage-reducing device on wet sites
Sets sharing a steel bench or structure can send current through chains, bearings and other paths
Clamp each work lead close to its own joint
A falling cylinder can snap its valve. CO2 is stored as a liquid and cools sharply as it expands, so regulators can freeze at high flows. CO2 and argon can collect in pits and tanks
Chain cylinders upright; use heated regulators or several cylinders for high flows; ventilate low places
Wire spools of 15 kg and more; heavy plate
Correct lifting; lifting aids; safety boots
Spatter travels far and lodges in cracks
Clear combustibles; extinguisher; fire watch after the work
Water, breaks in the shade, fans that do not blow across the arc

blocks.note: Overhead welding is where most burns happen. Before you start, check that your collar is closed, your sleeves and cuffs are done up, your cap covers your hair, and nothing (a pocket, a turn-up, a gap at the neck) can catch a falling ball of slag.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: Site work near the sea (wharves, jetties, coastal hotels) brings wind, salt and wet steel. Wind blows away a gas shield and pushes fume back at the welder, salt and moisture cause porosity, and wet conditions raise the risk of shock. Plan shelters, extraction and dry footing before the work starts.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: FCAW uses a **constant-voltage** power source. The wire feeder pushes a tubular wire through the gun at a set speed; the arc between the wire and the work melts it. The flux inside the wire forms slag over the weld and, depending on the wire, a gas shield too.

head: Type
How the weld is shielded
Best suited to
rows: Gas from a cylinder (CO2 or an argon/CO2 mix) plus slag from the core
Shop work; smooth arc; very good all-position welds with the right wire; tough weld metal
The core makes its own gas shield and slag; no cylinder
Site work in wind; portable; heavier fume; strict stick-out and polarity rules
Gas from a cylinder; the core is mostly metal powder, so there is very little slag
Long flat and horizontal welds; high deposition and little cleaning

head: Part
Its job
Points to check
rows: Constant voltage; you set the voltage
Rating plate and duty cycle; meters; connections tight
Sets the wire feed speed, which sets the current
Drive rolls: knurled or U-groove rolls for cored wire; pressure just enough to feed without crushing the wire
Guides the wire through the gun cable
Size to suit the wire diameter; clean; cable kept as straight as possible
Passes the current into the wire
Size matches the wire; replace when the bore is worn oval or spattered
Directs the shielding gas over the weld
Clean of spatter; the right size; no leaks
Return the current to the machine
On clean metal, close to the joint

ul: Most **gas-shielded** flux-cored wires (such as types T-1 and T-5) and metal-cored wires run on **DC electrode positive (DCEP)**.
Most **self-shielded** wires (such as types T-8, T-11 and T-GS) run on **DC electrode negative (DCEN)**. A few run on DCEP.
The wire label gives the polarity: always check it. Wrong polarity gives an unstable arc, spatter, poor fusion and porosity.

blocks.p: The **duty cycle** is the percentage of a 10-minute period that a set can weld at a given current without overheating. At a lower current it can weld for longer. A useful rule is that the current squared × the duty cycle stays roughly the same. For example, a set rated 300 A at 60% can weld at 250 A for about 60 × (300 ÷ 250)² = 60 × 1.44 ≈ 86% of the time. In a hot Jamaican shop, with the set in the sun, it will cut out sooner.

ul: **Wire feed speed**: release the drive pressure from the weld, or cut the wire at the tip, run wire out for a timed period, measure it and work out metres per minute. For example, 1.4 m in 7 seconds is 1.4 × 60 ÷ 7 = 12 m/min.
**Arc voltage**: measure with a meter between the gun (or the wire feeder) and the work, not only on the set's dial. Long or damaged cables and poor connections lose volts.
**Gas flow**: read with a flowmeter at the regulator, and check at the nozzle with a flow tester if porosity appears.

blocks.p: Mild steel flux-cored wires are classified by the AWS. The common (older) form looks like **E71T-1C-J H4**:

head: Part
Meaning
Example
rows: Minimum tensile strength of the weld metal, in tens of thousands of psi
Positions: 0 = flat and horizontal only; 1 = all positions
The usability type: how the wire runs, its slag, polarity and use
Shielding gas it was classified with: C = 100% CO2; M = an argon-rich mix (about 75–80% argon, the rest CO2)
The weld metal passed an impact (toughness) test at a lower, colder temperature than the standard requires
Diffusible hydrogen limit in the weld metal (mL per 100 g): H16, H8, H4; the lower the number, the lower the hydrogen

blocks.note: Newer AWS documents write the same information in a longer form (for example E71T1-C1A0-CS1-H8). Your WPS may use either; read it slowly, part by part, and match the wire label to it exactly.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Type
Shielding and polarity
Features and uses
rows: Smooth arc, low spatter, fast-freezing slag that holds the pool up; excellent all-position structural wire when the second digit is 1
Basic (lime) slag; very tough, crack-resistant weld metal; more spatter; mostly flat and horizontal unless classified for all positions
Multi-pass, all-position versions; good toughness; used for structural site work
General-purpose multi-pass site wire, with a thickness limit set by the maker
**Single-pass only**: thin sheet and galvanised work. In many passes its weld metal can crack or lose toughness
High deposition, flat and horizontal only
C = composite (metal-cored); M = mixed gas. Little slag, only small glassy islands; high deposition; good side-wall fusion; best for long flat and horizontal runs

ul: **100% CO2**: cheaper, deeper penetration, rougher arc and more spatter.
**Argon/CO2 mixes** (about 75–80% argon): smoother arc, less spatter, better bead shape, easier out of position.

A wire classified only with CO2 ("C") and run with an argon-rich mix gets more manganese and silicon into the weld metal, which can make it too strong and hard and less tough. A gas change is an essential variable: use only the gas the WPS lists.
Typical flow: about 15–25 L/min, as the WPS says. Too little lets air in; too much becomes turbulent and drags air in.
Set a short **pre-flow** so the joint is shielded before the arc starts, and a **post-flow** to protect the crater.
CO2 cylinders hold liquid CO2: use them upright so only gas is drawn off, and use a heated regulator for long runs at high flow.
Keep wire in its sealed packaging until it is used, in a dry store off the floor. The flux in the core can take up moisture, and rust on the wire causes porosity and poor feeding.
Do not leave spools on machines in the open yard or overnight in humid air; cover them or return them to the store. Jamaica's humidity rusts an exposed spool in days.
A rusty or damp spool is taken out of use and set aside or scrapped as the maker says. Do not try to dry flux-cored wire unless the maker gives a method.
Record the wire classification, diameter and **lot (batch) number**, and the gas, on the weld log for each joint, so a later fault can be traced to the batch.

head: Setting
Effect when it goes up
Points to know
rows: More current, more deposit, deeper penetration
On a constant-voltage set, wire feed speed sets the current
Longer arc, wider and flatter bead
Too high: spatter, undercut, porosity (especially with self-shielded wire). Too low: a ropey, convex bead and the wire stubbing into the plate
Longer CTWD: the wire is pre-heated more, so the current falls and penetration drops
Keep it steady at the maker's figure (often about 15–25 mm for gas-shielded wire; self-shielded wires have their own figures)
Faster: smaller, narrower bead, less heat
Too fast: undercut, poor fusion. Too slow: a large pool that runs ahead and causes lack of fusion and slag traps
Drag (pull) the gun about 10–15° on flat and horizontal work, so the slag stays behind the pool; point slightly upward for vertical-up

blocks.p: **Heat input** (kJ/mm) = volts × amps × 60 ÷ (travel speed in mm/min × 1 000). Too much heat input can lower the toughness of the weld and the heat-affected zone; too little can cause lack of fusion. Many WPSs give a maximum.

ul: **Preheat** slows the cooling of the weld, which lets hydrogen escape and stops the hard, crack-sensitive structure forming. The WPS gives the minimum, usually higher for thicker plate and stronger steels. Thick plate pulls heat away from the weld very fast, so it can need preheat even in Jamaica's heat.
Early in the morning, or after rain, steel can be wet with dew. Warm it to drive the moisture off before welding, whatever the preheat rule says.
The **maximum interpass temperature** stops heat building up pass after pass, which lowers toughness.
Check temperatures with **temperature-indicating crayons** (each melts at its stated temperature) or a contact thermometer, about 75 mm from the joint, or as the WPS says.

blocks.note: With crayons: stroke a preheat crayon on the steel; if it melts, the steel is at least that hot. Stroke an interpass-limit crayon; if it does not melt, the steel is below the limit and you may weld.
blocks.label: Tip

head: What you need
How
Worked example
rows: Total length of weld (all passes) ÷ travel speed
4 m of fillet in 2 passes at 320 mm/min: 8 000 ÷ 320 = 25 min
Cross-section area × length × 7.85 g/cm³; a fillet with leg L has an area of about L² ÷ 2
10 mm fillet: 50 mm² × 1 000 mm = 50 cm³ per metre × 7.85 ≈ 393 g per metre
Efficiency is roughly 80–90% for gas-shielded flux-cored, lower for self-shielded, higher for metal-cored: check the maker's figure
Duty cycle at a new current

blocks.note: Work every sum twice and check that it makes sense. A heat input of 11 kJ/mm or a 3-hour weld on a 300 mm bracket means a decimal point has slipped.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Bevel and fit the plates exactly as the WPS shows: the groove angle, root opening, root face and backing. For example, a WPS for 10 mm plate on backing might give a 45° included angle with about a 6 mm root opening. A smaller opening than the WPS gives leaves poor fusion into the root and the backing.
A **steel backing strip** must sit tight against both plates along its whole length. Any gap traps slag and leaves lack of fusion at the root.

Where the WPS allows, a one-sided root can be supported by **ceramic backing** tiles on adhesive tape, pressed tight and centred under the gap. They shape the root and are removed afterwards, so no backing is left on the job.
Clean the bevels, backing and about 25 mm each side to bright metal: rust, mill scale, paint, oil and moisture cause porosity.
Make tack welds with the same wire and to the same WPS as the main weld: tacks become part of the weld. On test plates, tack on the ends of the backing strip.
Use run-on and run-off tabs where the WPS asks, so the starts and stops are made off the joint.
Drag the gun about 10–15°, keep the CTWD steady, and keep the pool ahead of the slag.

Multi-pass horizontal fillets (2F) are built with stringer beads: the first in the root, then beads laid on the lower plate and on the upper plate in turn, each overlapping the one before by about half.
Horizontal grooves (2G) are filled with stacked stringers from the bottom upwards.
Set the wire speed and voltage at the lower part of the WPS range, and point the gun slightly upward.
The fast-freezing slag of an all-position rutile wire (such as E71T-1) forms a shelf that helps hold the pool up.
Root: a slight side-to-side movement, pausing briefly at each side so both edges fuse into the backing.
Fill passes: a weave or "shelf" motion, pausing at the toes to fill them and stop slag traps; keep each pass flat or slightly concave.
Cap: about 1–3 mm above the plate (within the code's limit), overlapping each bevel edge by about 1.5 mm, with no undercut.

blocks.note: Most structural procedures do not allow vertical-down on thick groove joints: the pool runs ahead of the arc and lies on the plate without fusing. Weld uphill unless the WPS says otherwise.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Keep the pool small: wire speed and voltage at the lower end of the range, and **narrow stringer beads** instead of a wide weave.
Use a slight drag angle and steady, slightly faster travel so the slag freezes behind the pool and supports it.
Keep each bead flat; a large pool sags and rolls over at the edges.
Take a comfortable, braced position, with full protection against falling slag.
Start a little ahead of the end of the last bead, or on a run-on tab, and bring the arc back so the start fuses.
Fill every crater (use the crater-fill setting if the set has one).

Remove all slag from every pass with a chipping hammer and wire brush, and grind humps and high spots before the next pass. Slag left on a pass does not all float out when it is remelted; it stays as an inclusion.

head: Defect
Main causes
Prevention
rows: Lost gas cover: wind, no pre-flow, blocked nozzle, leaks, too much suction, flow too high or too low
Damp or rusty wire; dirty or wet plate
Wrong CTWD or too high a voltage with self-shielded wire
Shelter the joint; set pre-flow; clean nozzles
Keep CTWD and voltage to the maker's figures
Humped passes leaving deep valleys at the toes
Travel too slow, pool running ahead
Grind humps; keep beads flat; pause at the toes
Correct travel speed and gun angle
Too little heat; travel too fast
Groove too narrow for the gun to reach
Root opening too small or root face too thick
Correct settings and aim at the root
A bead deeper than it is wide, often from high current in a narrow groove
Keep beads wider than they are deep; correct groove angle; follow preheat
Hydrogen cracking (beside the weld, may appear later)
Moisture in the wire, plate or gas
Thick or strong steel cooled fast
Dry wire with a low H rating; preheat; dry plate
Voltage or travel speed too high; wrong angle
Lower voltage; steady speed; correct angle; pause at toes
Voltage too low; travel too slow; pool too big out of position
Correct voltage; smaller beads; faster travel
Striking outside the joint; dirty nozzle; wrong settings or polarity
Strike in the joint; correct settings; clean equipment

ul: Inspect **before** (fit-up, root opening, backing tight, cleanliness, preheat), **during** (settings, interpass, cleaning between passes) and **after** welding (size, profile, undercut, cracks, porosity, cap height).
On a test plate, a crack or lack of fusion that shows on the surface fails it at once: it does not go on to bend testing.
Check fillet sizes with a fillet gauge: both legs must reach the size on the drawing.

flow: Mark the test plate with the welder's identity before welding so it cannot be swapped
After visual inspection, cut the strips from the places the code shows, away from the ends, which hold the starts and stops and are thrown away
Grind the cap and the backing strip flush with the plate, so the strip bends evenly and the weld itself is tested
Round off the long edges slightly, so a sharp corner cannot start a crack the weld did not cause
Bend each strip round the former in a guided bend jig, with guards in place
Examine the outside of the bend: the code limits the size of any open defect and the total

ul: **Face bend**: the cap side is stretched. **Root bend**: the root side is stretched. **Side bend**: the strip is turned on its side, testing the whole thickness; used for thicker plate.
A strip that opens along a bevel face with a smooth, shiny surface shows **lack of side-wall fusion**.

head: Test
How it is done
What it shows
rows: The upright plate is bent over, with the root in tension, until the weld breaks or folds flat
The fracture face shows root fusion, porosity and slag inside the weld
A slice is sawn across the weld, filed and sanded smooth, then etched with the etchant the Centre approves
The fusion boundary, root penetration, leg sizes, profile and any internal defects

blocks.note: Etchants are corrosive. Use them in a ventilated place with goggles, gloves and an apron, as the SDS says, and keep people clear when test pieces are broken.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: **Magnetic particle testing (MT)**: surface and near-surface cracks in steel.
**Ultrasonic testing (UT)**: internal defects, especially flat ones such as lack of fusion; common on structural groove welds.
**Radiography (RT)**: internal porosity, slag and lack of penetration.
Acceptance is decided by the inspector using the code's limits.

flow: Read the drawings, weld symbols and specification; list the joints, sizes, positions and tests
Get the approved WPS for each joint; check each welder's qualification and continuity, and give out joints to match
Check that the wire classification, diameter and lot, and the gas, match the WPS; check the wire is stored dry
Plan the welding sequence to control distortion, and use positioners so most welds are flat or horizontal
Set the hold points: fit-up, the first joint complete, after the root, final inspection
Brief the team on the WPS, the sequence, the hold points and the safety controls
Inspect the first joint fully before the rest go ahead
Check settings, preheat, interpass, cleaning and fit-up during the work; record each weld on the weld map
Repair any rejected weld to procedure, inspect it again, and complete the records for hand-over

blocks.p: Each pass heats the steel, which expands, and the weld metal shrinks as it cools. FCAW lays a lot of metal quickly, and many passes on one side of a joint pull it out of line: angular distortion of plates, bowing of beams, twisting of frames.

head: Method
How it helps
rows: Make welds the size on the drawing; extra metal means extra shrinkage
Use double-V or balanced joints where the design allows, and weld alternately on each side
Hold the parts firmly in line while they cool
Set the parts slightly out of line the opposite way, so shrinkage pulls them straight
Weld short runs balanced on each side, working from the centre outwards; back-step or skip on long welds
Keep to the WPS: higher heat input means more shrinkage

blocks.p: Check straightness and squareness with a straight edge, string line, square and diagonal measurements at set stages, and record the readings, so the sequence can be changed before the work goes too far.

ul: **Weld map**: a drawing with every weld numbered.
**Weld log**: for each weld, the welder, date, WPS, wire classification and lot, gas, the settings checked, and the inspection result.
**Test reports**: visual, bend, fillet break, macro, MT, UT and RT results.
**Repairs**: what was found, how it was repaired, and the re-inspection result.

blocks.note: Good records protect you: if a weld fails years later, the log shows which welder, which wire batch and which procedure made it, and that it was inspected.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it with your instructor.

ul: I can read a WPS and PQR and name the essential variables for FCAW.
I can check whether a welder's qualification covers the positions and thicknesses of a job.
I can name the AWS and ISO positions for groove and fillet welds.
I can control the fume, arc light, spatter, electrical, gas and heat hazards of FCAW.
I can explain gas-shielded, self-shielded and metal-cored wires and when each is best.
I can read a wire classification, including the position digit, the gas letter, J and H.
I can set the right polarity for a wire, and set up the drive rolls, liner, tip and nozzle.
I can check the real wire feed speed and arc voltage, and explain voltage drop.
I can explain the effect of wire speed, voltage, CTWD, travel speed and gun angle.
I can work out heat input, duty cycle, travel speed, arc time, weld metal and wire needed.
I can apply preheat and interpass limits and check them with crayons.
I can prepare groove joints on steel or ceramic backing and tack them correctly.
I can weld multi-pass groove and fillet joints in the flat, horizontal, vertical-up and overhead positions.
I can name the common FCAW defects, with their causes and cures.
I can prepare and judge bend, fillet break and macro tests.
I can plan a job, control distortion, lead the team and keep the weld records.

terms: A steel strip fixed under the root of a butt joint so it can be welded from one side
A strip cut across a weld and bent round a former to open up any defects
Tiles on tape that support and shape a one-sided root and are then removed
The copper part at the end of the gun that passes current into the wire
DC electrode negative / DC electrode positive
The share of the wire's weight that ends up as weld metal
The percentage of 10 minutes a set can weld at a given current without overheating
A change that needs a new or revised, qualified WPS
Bending a fillet test piece until the weld breaks, to inspect the fracture
A tubular wire filled with flux, making slag (and with some wires, gas)
The temperature of the joint just before the next pass is started
Weld metal lying against a bevel face without melting into it
A polished and etched cross-section of a weld, showing fusion and profile
A tubular wire filled mainly with metal powder, leaving very little slag
The part round the contact tip that directs the shielding gas
A short flow of shielding gas before the arc starts
Heating the steel before welding to slow cooling and prevent cracking
A procedure the code allows without a test, if it stays within the code's limits
Flux-cored wire that makes its own gas shield, used without a cylinder
The brittle coating left on top of a flux-cored bead
A bead made with little or no side-to-side movement
The record of each weld's welder, WPS, wire batch, gas and inspection result
Welding procedure specification: the written instructions for a weld

c1.title: A school canteen frame in Golden Grove
c1.text: Rushane leads a crew welding the steel frame of a school canteen in Golden Grove, St Thomas, in a covered shop. The WPS gives 1.2 mm E71T-1C wire with 100% CO2 on DCEP: 220–270 A, 24–28 V, travel speed 250–400 mm/min, and a maximum heat input of 1.8 kJ/mm. The FCAW set is rated 350 A at 60% duty cycle. One crew member, Garth, holds a qualification from tests in the 1G and 2G positions only.

c2.title: A fender frame on a jetty in Buff Bay
c2.text: A contractor is welding a steel fender frame onto a small jetty in Buff Bay, Portland. A strong sea breeze blows most days, and much of the welding is vertical and under the deck, where the air is still. The WPS calls for a self-shielded flux-cored wire for multi-pass joints, run on DCEN with a stick-out of 19–25 mm. The store has sent three wires: E71T-8, E71T-GS and E70T-4.

c3.title: Fillet test pieces at the Centre in Porus
c3.text: At a training centre in Porus, Manchester, a group welds 8 mm fillets on tee joints in 10 mm plate, in the vertical-up (3F) and overhead (4F) positions, with gas-shielded flux-cored wire. Afterwards they cut and etch macro sections and break other pieces. One macro shows the weld fused well into both plates, but the fusion stops about 1.5 mm short of the corner where the plates meet. On another piece the legs measure 9 mm on the base plate and 6 mm on the upright plate.

c4.title: Wire and feeding problems in Claremont
c4.text: Tanya is the supervisor at a fabrication shop in Claremont, St Ann, that uses 1.2 mm gas-shielded flux-cored wire. At one station the work-lead connection at the machine is loose and too hot to touch, and the arc keeps fluttering. At another the arc wanders and the wire leaves the gun off-centre; the contact tip's hole is worn oval. The engineer has also asked for very low-hydrogen weld metal on thick, heavily restrained column splices, and the long flat fillets on base plates are taking a long time to clean.

c5.title: Stiffeners on a crane runway beam in Grange Hill
c5.text: At a shop near Grange Hill, Westmoreland, Marlon leads three welders fitting 40 stiffeners to a crane runway beam with gas-shielded FCAW. Each stiffener has four single-pass 8 mm fillets, each 300 mm long. The welds are made in the horizontal position (2F) with the beam on its side, and one welder's fillets show a groove melted along the toe on the upright web.

questions.q: A welder runs a pass at 28 V and 250 A, travelling at 220 mm/min. What is the heat input, and what should Rushane do?
o: About 0.19 kJ/mm: well under the limit, so carry on
About 1.91 kJ/mm: over the limit, so travel faster
About 1.91 kJ/mm: within the limit, so carry on
About 19.1 kJ/mm: far over the limit, so stop the job
questions.why: Heat input = 28 × 250 × 60 ÷ (220 × 1 000) = 420 000 ÷ 220 000 ≈ 1.91 kJ/mm, above the 1.8 kJ/mm limit. The travel speed is also below the WPS's 250 mm/min, so speed up into the range.

questions.q: For about what percentage of the time can the set weld at 280 A?
o: About 60%
About 48%
About 75%
About 94%
questions.why: Duty cycle at the new current ≈ 60 × (350 ÷ 280)² = 60 × 1.5625 ≈ 94%. Working it in a straight line (60 × 350 ÷ 280 = 75%) underestimates it; the rule uses the square of the current ratio.

questions.q: Which of the canteen welds may Garth make?
o: Only the flat and horizontal welds
Any weld, as he is a qualified welder
Vertical welds, but not overhead ones
Only the welds his supervisor watches
questions.why: Tests in 1G and 2G generally qualify groove and fillet welds in the flat and horizontal positions only. Vertical or overhead welds need a 3G or 4G (or 3F and 4F) qualification.

questions.q: Why does the WPS use self-shielded wire on this job?
o: It gives far less fume than gas-shielded wire usually does
The breeze would blow a gas shield away from the arc
It is the only flux-cored wire that runs on DCEN
It needs no slag removal at all between the passes
questions.why: Self-shielded wire makes its own shielding from the core, so it copes with wind far better than a gas shield from a cylinder, and no cylinders need carrying onto the jetty. It makes more fume, not less.

questions.q: Which of the three wires suits the multi-pass vertical joints?
o: E71T-GS, because self-shielded wire suits any joint
E70T-4, because it lays metal down fastest
Any of them, as they are all self-shielded wires
E71T-8, a multi-pass, all-position wire
questions.why: E71T-8 is self-shielded, classified for all positions (the 1) and for multi-pass work. E71T-GS is for single-pass welds only, and E70T-4 is for flat and horizontal welding (the 0).

questions.q: A welder connects the gun to the positive terminal "as usual", and the arc is rough and the welds porous. What should he do?
o: Swap the leads so the gun is negative, as labelled
Turn the voltage well up until the arc steadies itself
Leave it, since all flux-cored wires run on DCEP
Fit a gas cylinder to protect the arc from the wind
questions.why: Most self-shielded wires, including E71T-8, run on DC electrode negative. On the wrong polarity the arc is unstable and the shielding does not work properly, so porosity follows. Always read the label.

questions.q: Under the deck the air is still, and the self-shielded wire makes heavy fume. What is the best control?
o: Weld faster so the fume has less time to build up
Turn the voltage down to make the arc smaller
Extraction at the arc, and respirators if needed
Short breaks in the fresh air every hour or so
questions.why: Self-shielded wire produces heavy fume containing manganese, and still air under a deck lets it build up. Capture it at the source with portable extraction, and add respirators as the risk assessment says.

questions.q: On the first macro, what does the gap in fusion at the corner of the plates show?
o: Undercut melted along the toe of the weld
Overlap of weld metal on the lower plate
Lack of fusion at the root of the weld
Excess convexity on the face of the weld
questions.why: The root of a fillet is the corner where the plates meet. Fusion stopping short of it means the weld did not reach the root; aim the arc into the root with enough current and the right angle.

questions.q: A broken fillet shows a line of small, round, shiny-walled holes along the middle of the weld. What fault is it, and what should be checked?
o: Slag inclusions: check the cleaning between passes
Lack of fusion: check the current was high enough
Porosity: check the gas cover, plate and wire
Cracking: check the preheat of the plate
questions.why: Round, smooth-walled holes are gas pores. Check for draughts, the gas flow and pre-flow, a blocked nozzle, and damp or rusty wire or dirty plate.

questions.q: The drawing asks for 8 mm fillets. What do the 9 mm and 6 mm legs show?
o: The weld passes, as the two legs average 7.5 mm
The weld passes, as the base plate leg is oversize
The weld is fine, since uneven legs are normal in 3F
The upright leg is undersize, so it fails
questions.why: Both legs must reach the size on the drawing. A 6 mm leg on an 8 mm fillet is undersize, so the weld must be repaired; aiming more evenly between the plates gives equal legs.

questions.q: How should the gun be used for the 3F vertical-up fillet?
o: Pointed down the joint, travelling quickly downwards
Pointed slightly up, weaving and pausing at the toes
Held level, with one wide weave and no pausing
Pulled hard back at 45°, with a very long stick-out
questions.why: Vertical-up with the gun pointed slightly upward lets the fast-freezing slag support the pool. Pausing at each toe fills it and avoids undercut and slag traps; downhill travel risks lack of fusion.

questions.q: What should be done about the hot, loose work-lead connection?
o: Turn the voltage up to make up for what is lost at the joint
Wrap the hot connection in insulating tape and carry on
Switch off, then clean and tighten or replace the connection
Pour water over the lug to cool it down between the runs
questions.why: A loose connection loses voltage and heats up, which makes the arc unstable and can melt the insulation or start a fire. Switch off, clean the contact faces and tighten or replace the lug before welding again.

questions.q: What should be done about the station where the arc wanders?
o: Replace the worn contact tip with one of the right size
Turn the wire speed down until the arc stays straight
Fit a larger nozzle so the gas covers the wandering arc
Lengthen the stick-out so the wire has room to settle
questions.why: A tip worn oval no longer guides the wire or passes current steadily, so the arc wanders and the wire leaves off-centre. Contact tips are consumables: replace them when worn or spattered.

questions.q: Which marking on the wire classification should Tanya look for to meet the engineer's request?
o: H4
J
M
questions.why: The H number is the maximum diffusible hydrogen in the weld metal, in mL per 100 g: H4 is the lowest of the common levels. J relates to impact toughness, and M to the shielding gas.

questions.q: Which change would most cut the cleaning time on the long flat fillets, if the WPS covers it?
o: Self-shielded wire, which leaves a thinner slag
A T-5 wire, which gives a basic slag
Pure argon, which stops slag forming
Metal-cored wire, which leaves very little slag
questions.why: Metal-cored wire has a core of mostly metal powder, so it leaves only small glassy islands, not a full slag cover, and lays metal fast on flat and horizontal work. It must be covered by a qualified WPS with the right gas.

questions.q: Each 8 mm fillet has a cross-section of about 32 mm². About how much weld metal do all the stiffener welds need? (Steel: 7.85 g/cm³.)
o: About 1.5 kg
About 12.1 kg
About 24.1 kg
About 121 kg
questions.why: Length = 40 × 4 × 300 = 48 000 mm. Volume = 32 × 48 000 = 1 536 000 mm³ = 1 536 cm³; × 7.85 ≈ 12 060 g, about 12.1 kg. Using 64 mm² (forgetting to halve 8 × 8) doubles it.

questions.q: The first stiffener has been welded. What should Marlon do before the other welders carry on?
o: Let them carry on and inspect all 40 stiffeners at the end
Inspect it fully and have it signed off at the hold point
Ask the welder whether he is happy with his own work
Paint it straight away so that it does not start to rust
questions.why: Inspecting the first joint (size, profile, undercut, fusion) at a hold point finds any problem with the settings or technique before it is repeated 39 more times.

questions.q: What is the most likely cause of the undercut on the web side of these fillets?
o: Voltage too low, which gives a narrow, ropey bead
Travel too slow, giving a large, heavy pool
Voltage too high, or aim too far up the web
Wire feed speed too low for the 8 mm leg
questions.why: Undercut on the upper toe of a horizontal fillet comes from too much voltage, travel that is too fast, or aiming too high on the upright plate. Lower the voltage within the WPS and aim more into the root.

questions.q: Why must a CO2 cylinder for FCAW be used standing upright?
o: It holds liquid CO2, which must not reach the regulator
An upright cylinder gives a higher gas flow rate
A cylinder lying down can never be chained safely
The gas inside separates into layers when it is laid flat
questions.why: CO2 is stored as a liquid with gas above it. Upright, only gas is drawn off; lying down, liquid can enter the regulator, freeze it and give an uneven flow. Chain cylinders upright.

questions.q: Why must all slag be removed from each FCAW pass, even though the next pass will remelt the surface?
o: Slag left in place makes the next arc start too hot
The inspector cannot measure a weld that has slag on it
Slag hides the colour of the weld beneath it
Not all slag floats out when remelted, so it is trapped
questions.why: Slag left on a pass, especially in the valleys at the toes, is not always melted and floated out by the next pass and stays as a slag inclusion, which shows on radiographs and bend tests.
